prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, which brought atomic frequency standards to the 10^-18 level of accuracy and stability

statement.case_for: Optical lattice clocks combine a clear conceptual invention, Katori's magic-wavelength lattice that cancels the light shift while many atoms are interrogated in parallel, with a decisive demonstration of what that idea makes possible, Ye's clocks at the 1e-18 level in accuracy and stability. It is laser cooling, trapping and spectroscopy producing a step change in what can be measured, which sits squarely in the tradition of precision-measurement prizes. The result has been confirmed by many independent laboratories and species, clock comparisons agree, the work already supports tests of constants and relativistic time dilation over centimetre scales, and a redefinition of the second is under discussion. The two-person credit is clean and maps onto concept plus demonstration. In the openings it was ranked first by Lindroth and by me, second by Danielsson and third by Pearce, so it has support across atomic physics, theory and instrumentation, and the atomic-structure arguments (polarizabilities, blackbody shifts, clock transitions) are ones that Lindroth and I can judge directly.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is distinctness from earlier recognition in the same lineage: the 2005 prize (Hall and Hansch, laser-based precision spectroscopy and the frequency comb) and the 2012 prize (Wineland and Haroche, control of single quantum systems, with ion clocks as a showcase). A committee could regard lattice clocks as a refinement of recognised enabling technology, and so far the fundamental-physics results from the clocks are null tests rather than discoveries. Credit is also not wholly exclusive: Lemonde, Ludlow and the PTB, NIST and SYRTE groups made important contributions, and the clocks rely on ultra-stable laser developments partly credited elsewhere. The redefinition of the second is prospective, not yet accomplished.

responses.point: Ranks magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene first: a theory prediction (Bistritzer and MacDonald) followed by the 2018 observation of correlated insulators and superconductivity, a new platform reproduced across many moire systems, with the superconducting mechanism still open.
responses.response: I agree that the prediction-to-observation chain is unusually clean and that the field has been reproduced widely; I ranked it eighth only because it lies outside my field and I do not claim to judge the physics of the correlated phases. My qualification is the one you yourself raise: eight years on, the origin of the superconductivity and the interplay of the correlated states are unresolved, and the theory attribution (Lopes dos Santos, Peres, Castro Neto) is open. A prize should rest on settled physics. Lattice clocks have two decades of independent confirmation and no comparable interpretive question, so I would let B009 mature a little longer, though I keep it as an alternative because the scientific merit is real.

responses.point: Ranks optical lattice clocks first, arguing that the work rests on detailed atomic-structure understanding and that the supplied credit supports a clean Katori and Ye pair, while noting that the 2005 and 2012 precision-measurement prizes raise a distinctness question.
responses.response: I largely agree and I take your atomic-structure judgement seriously, because the magic-wavelength condition and the blackbody and Stark shift budgets are what make the 1e-18 claims credible. On the distinctness question I would argue that 2005 recognised the comb as a ruler for optical frequencies and 2012 recognised the control of single ions, whereas the lattice clock is a different physical regime, a large ensemble of neutral atoms interrogated at once, which is what delivers the stability. I do concede that we should write the citation around the lattice concept so that it does not read as a third prize for the same lineage. Where I would qualify your view is the omission of Lemonde and Ludlow; I think the committee can defend a two-name award but should say so openly.

responses.point: Ranks the Higgs boson experimental discovery (B023) second, as an overdue instrument-driven landmark whose theory side was recognised in 2013, while ranking B026 first and lattice clocks third as a clean two-person configuration.
responses.response: I agree that the experimental Higgs discovery is a landmark and that its absence is awkward after 2013. My disagreement is on attribution: we would be crediting three founders and spokespeople as proxies for thousands of collaborators, and whether leadership of a proposal equals the decisive scientific contribution is exactly the standard we are asked to apply. That is a weaker fit with the individual-laureate rule than a two-person invention with well-delineated personal contributions. I also see B026 as a deserving candidate, but I share the concern raised by others about omitting Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang from the HgTe step. I would keep B023 as a strong long-term option, not as the configuration to settle on this year.

responses.point: Ranks active-matter hydrodynamics first as a conceptually unified new class of non-equilibrium statistical physics, while noting that Yuhai Tu is missing from the credit and that some predicted exponents are confirmed in only a few systems.
responses.response: I accept that the Toner-Tu and Vicsek ideas are original and have spread widely, and I am not competent to judge the renormalization-group arguments in detail. But I share your own reservation: with Tu missing the Toner-Tu theory would be recognised through one author, and quantitative confirmation is limited to a few experimental systems. That puts it behind candidates where a single measurable discovery can be stated and tested. I would be glad to hear how far you think the colloidal-roller and vibrated-rod experiments settle the exponents, since that would change my view of its maturity.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will treat lattice clocks as sufficiently distinct from the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize.
Whether a third name (for example Lemonde or Ludlow) is warranted, or whether the Katori and Ye pair is defensible against competing claims from PTB, NIST and SYRTE groups.
I rely on general knowledge, not independently verified record accuracy figures, and have not weighed the exact status of the second's redefinition.
How much weight to give to the unresolved superconducting mechanism in B009 versus its rapid reproduction and clean theory-experiment chain.
statement.conflict_note: Potential connections to flag: I spent a research stay in John Hall's laboratory in Boulder, and Hall is closely linked to the JILA precision-spectroscopy environment in which Jun Ye works, so a professional proximity to the B049 field exists although I have no documented collaboration with Katori or Ye. I also work in Lund atomic physics and quantum optics and have European quantum-memory collaborations that overlap with the community around Cirac and Zoller (B012), and I have been involved in WACQT, which touches superconducting-circuit quantum technology (B040). I would accept the committee's view on whether the Hall link requires recusal on B049.
